title: The golden calf (Exodus 32)
hookLine: Moses is late, so they melt their earrings into a god they can see

cards: Moses has gone up the mountain. A day passes. A week.
The cloud sits on the peak and nothing comes down. Forty days, the text says, and forty nights. Down in the camp, people start to talk.
Where is he? Is he dead up there? Who's in charge now?

A crowd gathers around Aaron, Moses' brother, left behind to lead, and they say, in the King James Bible: "Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him."

teach.b: Aaron doesn't argue. Bring me your gold earrings, he says. They pull them off, and he melts them down and shapes a calf.
The people cry out: "These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt." Not long before, they heard: no other gods, no carved images. But notice something else.
Aaron builds an altar and announces, tomorrow is a feast to the LORD. Some readers think they weren't trying to replace God at all.
They wanted a God they could see, one who couldn't go missing on a mountain: something to hold onto while they waited.
Up on the mountain, God tells Moses what's happening, and Moses pleads for the people, reminding God of his promises. And God relents.

teach.h: MOSES PLEADS, THEN BREAKS THE TABLETS.
teach.b: Then Moses comes down, sees the dancing, and in anger throws the stone tablets to the ground and breaks them at the foot of the mountain. Then a very human exchange.
Moses asks his brother, what did these people do to you, that you brought such a sin on them? And Aaron says, you know how they are. They gave me the gold.
"I cast it into the fire, and there came out this calf." As if it walked out by itself.

teach.h: UP, MAKE US GODS, WHICH SHALL GO BEFORE US.
teach.b: Christians have often read this chapter as a mirror. In that reading, an idol isn't only a statue.

It's whatever people grab hold of when God feels slow, when the answer is late, when the cloud on the mountain says nothing. And the story is honest that even Aaron, the future high priest, made it with his own hands.

how: Some Christian preachers use the golden calf to talk about modern idols such as money, success or control, and some churches read the story alongside the giving of the law.

games.q: you're Aaron. Moses has been gone forty days, and a crowd says, make us gods. what do you do?
o: tell them to wait for Moses.
climb the mountain to find him.
games.why: Aaron asks for the earrings and makes the calf. the future high priest gives the crowd what it wants, and later says it just came out of the fire.

practice: Think of the last time you waited for something that mattered, a test result, a reply, a decision, and what you reached for: food, the phone, control, a plan B.
Don't scold yourself; just see it clearly, then sit here empty-handed for a minute. If you pray, you can offer God the waiting itself.

wordCard.voice: Molten calf. The idol cast from the people's melted gold earrings while Moses was still on the mountain.

orig.note: Hebrew: a calf, a young bull. The text calls it a molten calf, cast from melted gold.

carryVoice: Your line: impatience makes idols. Waiting is hard, and the story knows it. See you tomorrow.
